allowed_claims: SavvyCal's Buffer Before setting enforces a minimum amount of time kept open before a new event.
SavvyCal's Buffer After setting enforces a minimum amount of time kept open after a new event.
SavvyCal's Minimum Notice setting requires a minimum amount of lead time before the start of a new event.
SavvyCal lets users toggle on Limit scheduling frequency and define one or more limits to cap the number of events booked through a link on a given day, week, or month.
To set up a custom domain, users create a CNAME record for their chosen subdomain (e.g., meet) pointing to custom.savvycal.com in their DNS settings.
Only one individual or team can be assigned to the root domain of a custom domain in SavvyCal.
Existing SavvyCal links continue to work at their original savvycal.com URL even after a custom domain is configured.

SavvyCal allows prospects to overlay their calendar on top of the user's to easily find mutual availability.
SavvyCal can generate a snippet of text to propose times in just seconds, and prospects can pick a time to meet in only two clicks.
SavvyCal can connect work, personal, and side-project calendars, check for conflicts across all of them, and set which calendar stores each meeting.
SavvyCal's meeting polls invite people to vote on the times that work best for them.
SavvyCal's meeting polls are available for free, with no ads.
SavvyCal is backed by a 30-day money-back guarantee.
The Basic plan includes unlimited links.
The Premium plan adds custom domains on top of everything in Basic.
Reminders & Workflows automation is included in both the Basic and Premium plans.
With Calendar Overlay, the recipient can view their calendar events on top of the sender's scheduling link.
SavvyCal lets users adjust the colors, banner image, and avatar that appear on their scheduling links.
SavvyCal lets users host their scheduling links on their own custom domain.
SavvyCal's Buffers & Limits feature prevents meeting overload and caps meeting quantity per day, week, and month.
SavvyCal's Time Blocking feature lets users budget their time using calendar events, and SavvyCal honors those preferences.
SavvyCal's Preferred Slots feature encourages people to schedule meetings at the optimal time of day and clustered near other meetings.

brief.promise: SavvyCal is worth evaluating when a founder wants a free, ad-free meeting poll for the simple job of letting people vote on suitable times.
brief.orientation: For a founder who books his own client, partner and investor calls, SavvyCal is a scheduling-link tool whose link shows a week view the recipient can lay their own calendar over, with per-link buffers, notice and volume limits that govern when a booking is allowed.
brief.arc: Move the reader from seeing scheduling software as unnecessarily elaborate for agreeing on one time to recognizing one narrow SavvyCal use case they can evaluate: invite people to vote on suitable times with a free, ad-free meeting poll.
brief.sequence_rationale: This single email replaces the invalid settings-preview proposition with a smaller decision supported by P4 and documented product evidence. The fixed /signup destination still requires account creation, but the promised payoff is now limited to evaluating a meeting-poll capability explicitly documented as free and ad-free. The email must not imply a pre-signup preview, effortless setup, or evidence that recipients experience polls as more collaborative.

emails.selection_reason: The audience research identifies occasions when scheduling software feels excessive for simply agreeing on one time. SavvyCal's documented free, ad-free meeting polls give this self-directed founder a specific and bounded reason to create an account and evaluate the product.
emails.argument_issue: The destination requires account creation, and no supplied evidence establishes a pre-signup poll preview, the effort required to configure a poll, or how recipients will perceive the experience.
emails.job: Earn account creation for a bounded evaluation of SavvyCal's free meeting polls.
emails.single_idea: When the job is simply to settle on a time, SavvyCal offers free, ad-free meeting polls that let people vote on the times that work for them.
emails.felt_need: Scheduling tools are experienced as overkill for the simple case of agreeing on one time, with useful features gated behind extra cost or extra tools.
emails.mechanism: SavvyCal meeting polls present candidate times and invite people to vote on the options that work best for them. The supported evaluation is limited to whether this free, ad-free format suits the founder's occasional group-coordination needs.
emails.belief_shift: Before: evaluating another scheduling product only makes sense for replacing the founder's entire booking workflow. After: SavvyCal can be evaluated through one narrower job—using a free, ad-free poll to collect votes on meeting times.
must_not_say: Do not claim meeting polls eliminate scheduling back-and-forth, guarantee agreement, save a measured amount of time, or require no configuration.
Do not claim recipients find meeting polls more personal, collaborative, polite, or less status-asserting than scheduling links.
Do not state or imply that this recipient currently uses Calendly or any other named scheduling product.
Do not claim the reader has abandoned a booking link, experienced seven meetings in a day, or had a booking disrupt an important meeting.
Do not promise a pre-signup poll preview or an inspectable recipient experience before account creation.
Do not claim account creation is unnecessary, instant, or requires no credit card.
Do not generalize the free offer beyond SavvyCal meeting polls or imply that every SavvyCal feature is free.

Do not introduce Calendar Overlay, proposed-time snippets, buffers, frequency limits, custom domains, branding, workflows, integrations, paid bookings, pricing, customer counts, or competitor comparisons.
Do not promise effortless migration, automatic transfer of existing links, or compatibility with the reader's current tools.

Free, ad-free meeting polls address only the simple polling use case; they do not establish a lightweight flow elsewhere in the product or resolve the broader social objections to sending scheduling links.

Proposed-time snippets and meeting polls are documented alternatives to pasting a link, but it remains a scheduling tool and no selected evidence shows cold-outreach or high-trust recipients experience it as collaborative.

Free ad-free polls, reminders/workflows and unlimited links on Basic cover part of the complaint, but custom domains and paid bookings are Premium-only additions, the selected evidence gives no plan prices (only 'save 2 months' annually), and no lightweight flow outside meeting polls avoids configuring a link.
emails.objection: Do I need to pay for a full scheduling setup just to coordinate one meeting? Answer narrowly: SavvyCal documents its meeting polls as free and ad-free, while signup and any configuration effort remain part of the evaluation.
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact, friendly, and lightly playful; keep the invitation small and concrete.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether SavvyCal's free meeting-poll format is useful for occasions when several people need to settle on a time.
emails.next_step_value: After creating an account, the reader can evaluate a documented meeting-poll capability that invites people to vote on suitable times and is available free without ads.
emails.next_step_limit: The /signup step requires account creation and offers no verified pre-signup poll preview. It does not establish setup effort, recipient sentiment, agreement rates, suitability for the founder's full scheduling workflow, or the terms of other SavvyCal features.
emails.subject_strategy: Earn the open with the narrow utility of a free meeting poll for agreeing on a time, without positioning it as a wholesale scheduling-tool replacement or presuming dissatisfaction with an installed product.

brief.voice_notes: Use short, plain-spoken sentences and SavvyCal's concrete you/we rhythm. Keep the scope deliberately small; avoid aggressive productivity claims and invented stories about the recipient's calendar.

intelligence.selected_audience: A bootstrapped software founder who sends his own calendar link to clients, partners and investors and winces slightly every time he pastes it
partial_caveats_injected: The selected evidence licenses only a changed booking surface (recipient overlays their own calendar, personalized and branded link); it contains no evidence that recipients read such a link as less status-asserting, and the researched objection is to the act of sending a link at all.

Proposed-time snippets and meeting polls are documented alternatives to pasting a link, but it remains a scheduling tool and no selected evidence shows cold-outreach or high-trust recipients experience it as collaborative.

These mechanisms govern when and how often anyone may book (notice, buffers, day/week/month caps, honored time blocks, preferred slots) and allow separate links per relationship; prioritising slots by who the booker is is not established by the selected evidence, so the 'some people matter more' half of the problem stays unaddressed.

Free ad-free polls, reminders/workflows and unlimited links on Basic cover part of the complaint, but custom domains and paid bookings are Premium-only additions, the selected evidence gives no plan prices (only 'save 2 months' annually), and no lightweight flow outside meeting polls avoids configuring a link.
